extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing when and how a patent owner may seek a re-issue to correct, enlarge, or amend claims (including doctrines of laches, abandonment, notice, and intervening rights). Focuses on timing, evidence of inadvertence, public dedication, and limits on expanding claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt examination and duty to correct
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor receives his patent, it is his duty to examine it promptly, see that his invention is properly described, and that his Claims are broad enough to embrace it in all its scope; failure to do this is a dedication to the public of so much of his invention as is not covered by his Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must act with reasonable diligence and speed; unnecessary laches or delay affects right to alter or re-issue. Cases: Wollensak v. Reiher; Miller v. Brass Co.; Hahn v. Harwood. If upon mere reading it is obvious he is entitled to broader claims, he must apply speedily; failure may be treated as abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue available only for inadvertence, accident, or mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issues for the enlargement of Claims should be the exception and not the rule; enlargement can only be done when an actual mistake has occurred — not from a mere error of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will require clear proof of inadvertence/accident/mistake. Miller v. Brass Co. emphasizes re-issues are to correct real mistakes. If delay suggests the patentee simply exercised poor judgment, re-issue to enlarge is not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of claims being too narrow vis-à-vis public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent (and specifically its Claim) operates in law as a disclaimer of what is not claimed; what is not claimed is public property and the public is notified by the patent of the patentee's claimed scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where omitted matter is clearly described but not claimed, the law presumes the inventor intended to abandon it or withhold it for a future patent; the public may rely on that implied disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: No re-issue to claim matter clearly described but omitted after unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: No re-issue can be allowed to claim matter clearly described in the original patent but omitted from its Claims, unless the re-issue is applied for within a reasonable time after the grant of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay converts the presumption of inadvertence into a presumption of intentional exclusion/abandonment. Authorities: Ives v. Sargent; Gage v. Kellogg; Reed v. Chase; Wooster v. Handy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two years/public use as strong evidence of abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Two years' public enjoyment/use of an invention with the consent and allowance of the inventor is evidence of abandonment and a bar to claiming that matter by re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two years is the usual limit suggested; but it is not absolute — courts consider all circumstances. Ex parte Flynn and other cases discussed. Also a new independent application for the omitted matter within two years can rebut the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable time / no fixed limit
rubrics_metrics.description: No invariable rule can be laid down as to what is reasonable time within which the patentee should seek correction of a claim considered too narrow; reasonable time depends on the particular facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh factors (commercial importance, knowledge of defect, intervening rights). Cases: Hahn v. Harwood, Stutz v. Armstrong, Odell v. Stout. Two years is a common benchmark but not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches and delay as bar to re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary delay in seeking re-issue is acquiescence in the patent as allowed and is evidence of abandonment of the omitted invention; laches should be strictly applied to re-issues enlarging scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where delay has induced the public to rely on the implied disclaimer, courts may declare re-issue illegal and void. See Giant Powder Co., Turrell v. Bradford, Consolidated Fruit Jar Co. v. Bellaire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater discrepancy shortens allowable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the discrepancy between the original claim and the matter sought to be added by re-issue, the shorter should be the time allowed to correct it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the enlargement is large/obvious, only a very short delay will be excused; courts will be stricter. See Cahn v. Harwood and related commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay shorter when defect is apparent on face of patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defect is apparent on the face of the patent and can be discovered upon first inspection, there can be no valid excuse for delay in seeking correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miller v. Brass Co. and other cases hold that defects discoverable from opening the patent cannot be excused by delay. The spectacle of an obvious defect defeats later re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening/adverse rights defeat re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether adverse rights have arisen since the original patent was granted is important to re-issue; intervening rights (public use/patent by another) can bar re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether third parties have begun using the omitted matter or another patent claims it; such rights support finding abandonment and prohibit re-issue. See Turrell v. Bradford; cases on sub-combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay excused where defect not clearly described or discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the omitted matter was only suggested or not clearly described in the specification, so that the defect was not evident to the inventor upon mere inspection, mere delay does not raise presumption of intentional exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee's obligation to amend arises only after circumstances direct attention to the error; upon notice he must amend within reasonable time. Cases: section §691 discussion, Poppenhusen v. Falke, Hartshorn v. Eagle Shade Roller Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere delay alone does not prove intentional exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An intention to exclude is never inferred from mere delay alone where the omitted matter was merely indicated or not clearly described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not infer bad faith from delay unless other evidence shows intentional exclusion; ambiguity/complexity may entitle patentee to more indulgence. See §692 and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot be used to appropriate later-developed forms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an abuse to wait until others have produced new forms or improvements and then under pretence of inadvertence apply for an enlargement to embrace these new forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue statute is to protect against accidents/mistakes, not to permit persistent expansion to cover subsequent improvements. Such conduct may render re-issue void. See commentary about abuse and Miller v. Brass Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot expand claim after long lapse (e.g., eight years) except in peculiar cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot expand a Claim after eight years except in peculiar circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long lapses (multi-year) are strong evidence against allowance; Tuttle v. Loomis cited for eight-year limit caveat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee charged with notice of patent contents upon issue and reasonable diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is chargeable with notice of what the patent contains and is held to reasonable diligence; ignorance of law is no excuse for delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts expect patentees to know what they have claimed; reasonable care and inspection are required. Cases: Westem Union Tel. Co. v. B. & O. Tel. Co.; Ives v. Sargent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery mode does not alter right to re-issue if inadvertence shown
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode in which discovery of a mistake is made does not affect the right to re-issue when the error was inadvertent; judicial construction that first reveals the defect can justify a surrender and re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If judicial interpretation shows the patent failed to cover the invention, that disclosure may justify re-issue to correct inadvertent description. See Poppenhusen v. Falke and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue limited when it would prejudice public or intervening rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Where delays work an equitable estoppel or prejudice rights of the public and third parties, re-issue may be refused; the rule favors the public where delay has misled reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts balance equities; unavoidable delay may be excused but avoidable delay leading to prejudice bars re-issue. Consolidated Fruit Jar Co. v. Bellaire Stamping Co. cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: New separate application as alternative to re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: If the omitted matter is claimed in a new application filed before two years of public use or sale have elapsed, the new application is independent and must be judged on its merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a new patent application for omitted matter within the two-year period can rebut presumption of abandonment and operates independently of the original patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner/Court review and limits on grant of re-issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is manifest from the patent itself, compared with the original patent and record, that the Commissioner disregarded the rules of law in granting re-issue, the re-issue will be considered void to that extent; courts review legality not just facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issues granted contrary to legal limits (e.g., to enlarge improperly after intervening rights) may be declared void as a matter of law. See Mahn v. Harwood and other authority.
